title: The Old Room
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of self-encounter and quiet fatherhood
excerpt: His grandmother had left him the house. He had not seen her in eighteen years. On his first afternoon in the small house on Nagymezo Street, he climbed the stairs to the small back bedroom where he had slept every summer of his childhood. It was as he had left it. He sat on the bed. The mattress was warm.

chapters.title: The House on Nagymezo Street
chapters.body:
His grandmother had left him the house.

Tamás Kovács was forty-six, and he had, in the third week of March, received a small letter from a small lawyer's office in Budapest informing him that his grandmother — his father's mother, Magda Kovács — had died at ninety-one, in her sleep, in the small house on Nagymezo Street where she had lived for the whole of her adult life, and had left the house, along with a small quantity of savings, to Tamás.

Tamás had, at the small letter, been surprised in the specific small quiet way of a man whose adult family relations had, over the years, become distant. He had not seen his grandmother in eighteen years. He had, over the last two decades, sent her a small annual Christmas card, and had, at long intervals, spoken to her briefly by telephone. He had not, at any point in his adult life, expected to inherit anything from her. He had, if he had thought about it at all, assumed that whatever she had left would go to his father, and after his father to Tamás's older sister, in the specific small ordinary way of Hungarian family inheritance.

His father had died six years earlier. His sister had died four years after that.

Tamás had, on receiving the small letter, understood that he was, as of that Wednesday, the last remaining member of his father's family.

He had lived, throughout his adult life, in London. He had, at twenty-three, moved there for a small job in a small architectural firm, and had, over the years, become the sort of quiet man who — through a small combination of small career choices and small personal reluctances — had never entirely committed to going back and had never entirely committed to staying. He had, in the twenty-three years of his London life, been married for eight and divorced for six. He had no children. He worked, at forty-six, as a small consultant on small heritage projects, in the specific small quiet way of a man who had made his small living out of preserving other people's small pasts.

He had, on receiving the small letter, arranged to fly to Budapest.

He had gone in the second week of April, on a small Thursday morning, and had, on arriving, taken the small train from the airport to Keleti station, and had, from Keleti, walked the small twenty minutes to the small house on Nagymezo Street where his grandmother had lived and where he had, throughout his childhood, spent every summer of his life until he was fifteen.

He had, standing at the small gate of the small house on that Thursday afternoon in April, understood two things.

He had understood, first, that the house looked exactly as it had when he was a child.

He had understood, second, that this was not exactly correct.

Houses that had, for eighteen years, been the sole habitation of a woman in her seventies and eighties should, on any ordinary inspection, show the small signs of that habitation. The small paint on the small window frames should have faded. The small garden should have grown up. The small hedge between the small path and the small street should have thickened. None of these had happened. The paint was fresh. The garden was mown. The hedge was clipped in the specific small careful way his grandmother had, throughout his childhood, insisted upon.

The house looked, in the specific small careful way, as though his grandmother had prepared it for him.

He had, standing at the small gate, understood that this was, in some small careful way, correct.

He had opened the small gate.

He had walked up the small path.

He had, at the small door, used the small brass key the small lawyer's office had sent him.

The small door had opened without any of the small careful reluctance one might have expected from a small door that had, for two weeks since his grandmother's death, been closed.

He had walked inside.

—

The small entrance hall had smelled of his grandmother.

He had, at the specific small smell — a specific small combination of the wax his grandmother had used on the small wooden floors, and the small dried lavender she had kept in a small bowl on the small hall table, and the specific small trace of the small perfume she had worn since before Tamás had been born — stopped just inside the small door.

He had stood in the small hallway for perhaps a full minute.

He had, at last, closed the small door behind him.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man walking through the small house of his own childhood, gone slowly through the small rooms.

The small sitting room had been as he remembered it. His grandmother's small green armchair, with its specific small worn place at the small right arm. His grandfather's — his grandfather had died when Tamás was seven — larger brown armchair on the other side of the small coffee table. The small bookshelf along the small east wall, with his grandmother's small collection of Hungarian and German novels arranged in the specific small careful way she had, throughout her life, arranged them: alphabetically by author, without regard to language, on the theory that a small woman who spoke both languages had no need to keep them separate.

The small kitchen had been as he remembered it. The small square wooden table where his grandmother had, throughout his childhood summers, taught him to peel small potatoes and to chop small carrots and to make the small small dumplings for the small chicken soup she had, on his last day of every summer, always made for him.

The small dining room had been as he remembered it.

The small stairs, at the back of the small hallway, had been as he remembered them.

He had, at the small foot of the small stairs, hesitated.

The small stairs had led up to the small second floor, on which had been the small bathroom, his grandmother's small bedroom, and the small back bedroom that had, throughout his childhood, been the small bedroom his grandmother had kept for him.

He had, throughout his childhood, spent every summer of his life in that small back bedroom.

He had, at fifteen, on the last summer he had come to the small house, slept in it for the last time.

He had, on the last morning of that last summer, taken his small suitcase down the small stairs, and had, at the small door, said the small goodbye to his grandmother that he had not, at the time, known was going to be the last time he stayed in the small back bedroom.

He had not, at any point in the thirty-one years since, come back to sleep in it.

He had, at the small foot of the small stairs on that Thursday afternoon in April, understood that this was, at last, the moment.

He had climbed the small stairs slowly.

He had, at the small top of the small stairs, walked past his grandmother's small bedroom — the small door had been closed, in the specific small careful way she had always closed it — and had walked to the small door at the end of the small hallway.

He had, at the small door, put his hand on the small brass handle.

He had, for a moment, closed his eyes.

He had opened the small door.

—

The small back bedroom had been as he had left it.

It had been exactly as he had left it. It had been, on his careful inspection over the following several minutes, so exactly as he had left it that he had begun, at first, to think that he had, in the intervening thirty-one years, misremembered the small details, and had, in his memory, adjusted them so as to match his current perception.

But it had, on his careful inspection, been the room he remembered.

The small single bed had been in the specific small corner where his grandmother had always kept it. The small blue coverlet — the specific small blue coverlet with the specific small pattern of white flowers — had been on the small bed. The small desk under the small window. The small wooden chair with the specific small carved back. The small chest of drawers along the small west wall. The small framed print of the small castle at Visegrád above the small bed — a small print he had, at eight, admired, and had, at eight, asked his grandmother whether he could keep in the small back bedroom instead of the small print of the small church at Esztergom that had been there before.

The small print of Visegrád had, throughout his subsequent childhood, been the small print above the small bed.

It had been the small print above the small bed on that Thursday afternoon in April.

He had, standing in the small doorway, understood that his grandmother had, throughout the eighteen years since he had last visited her, kept the small back bedroom exactly as he had, at fifteen, left it.

He had, standing in the small doorway, felt a specific small chill pass through him.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man doing a small careful inspection, walked into the small back bedroom.

He had walked to the small chest of drawers. He had, in the specific small careful way, opened the small top drawer. Inside had been, in the small careful arrangement of his fifteen-year-old self, a small collection of specific small objects: three small pencils, a small sharpener, a small notebook with his small handwriting on the small first page, a small green pocketknife his father had given him at twelve, and a small pair of clean cotton socks he had, at fifteen, on the last morning, forgotten to pack.

The small socks had, in the specific small careful way, been washed. Someone had, at some point in the thirty-one years, washed them and returned them to the small drawer.

He had, in the specific small careful way, closed the small drawer.

He had walked to the small bed.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man doing a small necessary check, sat on the small edge of the small bed.

He had noticed, at the small moment of sitting, something.

The small mattress had, on his sitting, been warm.

He had, sitting on the small edge of the small bed, held very still.

The small mattress had, in the specific small unambiguous way, been warm. It had been warm in the specific small careful way of a small mattress on which someone had, in the last quarter of an hour, been lying.

Tamás had, sitting on the small edge of the small bed, understood two things simultaneously.

He had understood, first, that no one had been in the house when he had arrived. He had walked through the small ground floor. He had not, at any point in his walking, seen or heard any small evidence of a small other occupant.

He had understood, second, that the small mattress was, unmistakably, warm.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man in a small strange situation, gotten up slowly. He had gone to the small door. He had, at the small door, looked back at the small bed. The small blue coverlet had been perfectly smooth. The small pillow had been perfectly plumped. There had been, on the small bed, no specific small visible evidence of a small occupant.

But the small mattress, under the small coverlet, had been warm.

He had, at the small door, walked out of the small back bedroom.

He had, at the small top of the small stairs, walked to his grandmother's small bedroom. He had opened the small door.

The small bedroom had been empty.

He had walked to the small bathroom. He had opened the small door.

The small bathroom had been empty.

He had gone downstairs. He had, at the small ground floor, walked through the small rooms again. He had walked through the small sitting room, and the small dining room, and the small kitchen. He had checked the small pantry. He had checked the small storage cupboard under the small stairs.

The small house had been, on the specific small careful inspection, entirely empty.

He had, at last, gone into the small kitchen. He had, at the small kitchen table, sat down.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man permitting himself to think slowly through a small strange thing, considered.

He had considered that the small warm mattress could have had a small ordinary explanation. A small trapped column of afternoon sun through the small window might, for reasons of a small specific alignment, have been warming the small bed. The small central heating might, for reasons he did not immediately understand, have been on and might have been warming the small mattress from below. His own small tired body might, at the specific small hour of arrival after a small flight and a small train, have been unreliable in its small assessment of what warm meant.

He had, considering these, understood that none of them quite worked. The small window of the small back bedroom faced west and would not, at four o'clock on an April afternoon, have received the specific small angle of sun that would have warmed the specific small area under the coverlet. The small central heating in the small house had been, on his walking through, off — the small radiators were cold to the touch. His own small tired body was, on inspection, not producing any small misperception; he could, at any small moment, still feel the specific small memory of the specific small warmth against the small pads of his fingers.

The small mattress had been warm because a small person had, in the specific small time before his arrival, been lying on it.

Tamás had sat, at the small kitchen table, for a long time.

He had, at last, gotten up. He had gone into the small hallway. He had picked up his small suitcase, which he had, on entering, left by the small door. He had climbed the small stairs.

He had, at the small door of the small back bedroom, hesitated.

He had, at last, opened the small door.

He had walked in.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man deciding to spend the small night in the small room, put down his small suitcase at the small foot of the small bed.

He had, before doing anything else, walked to the small bed and had, in the specific small careful way, put his small hand on the small mattress under the small coverlet.

The small mattress had been cold.

chapters.title: Small Occupants
chapters.body:
He had not, that first evening, slept in the small bed.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man not entirely sure what he was doing, made himself a small dinner from the small provisions he had brought in his small bag, and had, at ten o'clock, laid out a small sleeping arrangement on the small sofa in the small sitting room downstairs, and had, at ten-thirty, gone to sleep on the small sofa.

He had, at three in the morning, been woken.

He had been woken by a small sound.

He had, lying on the small sofa in the specific small dark of the small sitting room, listened.

The small sound had come from above him. It had come, unmistakably, from the small back bedroom on the small second floor. It had been the specific small sound of a small person turning over in a small bed.

He had lain very still.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man listening to a small strange sound in his grandmother's small house, tried to identify what the small sound could have been.

He had, over the following minute, been unable to identify it as anything but what it had been: the small unmistakable sound of a small mattress and a small coverlet being disturbed by a small ordinary movement of a small ordinary body.

He had, at last, gotten up.

He had gone into the small hallway. He had climbed the small stairs slowly.

He had, at the small top of the small stairs, stood in the small darkness and had listened.

The small house had been silent.

He had walked, quietly, to the small door of the small back bedroom.

He had, at the small door, put his small hand on the small brass handle.

He had held it for a very long moment.

He had, at last, turned it slowly.

He had opened the small door.

The small back bedroom had been, so far as he could see in the small pale light of the small streetlamp coming through the small window, empty.

The small bed had been made in the specific small careful way of a small bed that had not been disturbed. The small blue coverlet had been perfectly smooth. The small pillow had been perfectly plumped.

But the small pillow had, on the specific small careful look, had a small small indentation in it. As if, in the small few seconds between the small sound of the small movement and the small opening of the small door, the small occupant had, in the specific small careful way, gotten up. Had straightened the small coverlet. Had almost, but not quite, plumped the small pillow.

Tamás had, at the small door, understood something.

He had understood that whatever was in the small back bedroom did not, in the specific small careful way, want him to see it.

He had understood, further, that whatever it was had been in the small back bedroom for some considerable time. Since, in fact, some point in his own childhood.

He had, standing at the small door in the small dark at three in the morning, said quietly, in Hungarian:

*Hello.*

There had been no answer.

He had said, more quietly: *are you there.*

There had been, at that question, a small change in the small quality of the small quiet in the small back bedroom. It had, at his question, altered. It had, in the specific small careful way, *attended.*

He had said: *are you a child.*

There had been no answer. But the small quality of attention had, at the question, become more careful — had, in the specific small way, become more considered.

He had said, in the specific small quiet way of a man who had, over the last several hours, been thinking about a specific small possibility: *are you me.*

The small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, at that question, done something Tamás had not, at any point in his forty-six years, felt.

It had, in the specific small careful way, *contracted.* It had drawn itself into itself. It had, in the small way of a small child who had, in a small game, been discovered, gone quiet.

Tamás had, at the small door of his childhood bedroom in his grandmother's small house at three in the morning of a Thursday in April, understood that the small occupant of the small back bedroom was, in some specific small strange way, himself.

Himself at some earlier age.

Himself as a small child.

—

He had, that morning, at five, gone downstairs and had made himself a cup of coffee, and had, at the small kitchen table, considered.

He had understood that the small occupant of the small back bedroom was, in some specific way he could not entirely articulate, a version of himself from his childhood. He had understood this from the specific small quality of the way the small attention in the small back bedroom had responded to his question. The specific small careful contraction. The small quiet of a small child who had been recognized.

He had considered what version of himself.

He had considered that the small back bedroom had, throughout his childhood, been the small bedroom he had slept in each summer. He had considered that his grandmother had, in the eighteen years since his last summer visit, kept the small bedroom exactly as he had, at fifteen, left it. He had considered that whatever was in the small back bedroom now was, in some small strange way, the specific small child who had, throughout those summers, slept in it.

He had understood, in the specific small careful way, that the small child was probably not fifteen. The small quality of attention had felt younger. Perhaps eight. Perhaps ten.

He had considered how this had happened.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man considering an impossible thing, tried various explanations. The small ghost of his own childhood self, somehow left behind. The small careful preservation of some specific small memory by his grandmother, that had, over eighteen years of being alone with the small back bedroom, become in some small way substantial. The small careful attention of a house that had, throughout his childhood, been the site of his summers, that had, in the specific small way of certain small houses, come to hold onto something.

None of the explanations had, in the specific small careful way, entirely satisfied.

He had, at the small kitchen table, understood that he was not, on the whole, going to be able to explain what was in the small back bedroom.

He had, however, been able to consider what to do about it.

He had considered leaving.

He had considered — briefly — closing the small house up, telling the small lawyer that he did not, after all, want to keep the small property, arranging for the small house to be sold, and returning to London on the next flight, without ever setting foot again on the small stairs.

He had understood, considering this, that he was not going to do it.

He had understood that he was not going to do it because he had, over the last twelve hours, come to understand that there was, in the small back bedroom, a small version of himself who had, for eighteen years, been alone there. A small child. A small specific small child who had, at some point, been him.

He had understood that he was not going to leave the small child alone.

—

He had, that afternoon, at three, gone into the small back bedroom.

He had done it in the specific small careful way of a man who had been thinking about what he was going to do for the last several hours. He had brought with him a small book he had found on his grandmother's small shelves — a small collection of Hungarian folk tales, of the small kind his grandmother had, throughout his childhood, read to him at the small end of long summer afternoons — and he had, on entering the small back bedroom, gone to the small wooden chair with the specific small carved back, and had sat down.

He had, in the specific small careful way, opened the small book.

He had, in the specific small careful voice of a man reading aloud to a small quiet listener, begun to read.

He had read for perhaps ten minutes.

He had, at the end of ten minutes, closed the small book. He had, in the specific small careful way, said, into the small back bedroom:

*I will come back tomorrow. I will read some more.*

He had, in the specific small careful way, walked out of the small back bedroom.

He had, on the small landing, felt the small quality of attention in the small back bedroom behind him, and had understood — in the specific small way one understood such things — that the small occupant had, throughout the ten minutes, been listening. Had, in the specific small careful way, been sitting on the small bed under the small print of Visegrád, and had, in the specific small way, been listening to a small careful older voice reading a small careful old story.

Tamás had, on the small landing, felt the small warmth of a small remembered kindness.

He had understood that his grandmother had, throughout his childhood, read to him in the specific small back bedroom in exactly the specific small way he had, that afternoon, been reading to the small occupant.

He had understood that he was, in the specific small careful way, doing for the small version of himself what his grandmother had, throughout his childhood, done for him.

He had gone downstairs.

—

He had, over the following weeks, developed a small careful routine.

He had, in the mornings, done the small ordinary work of settling the small estate. He had met with the small lawyer. He had gone through the small papers. He had, at the small bank, transferred the small savings. He had, on a small small Tuesday, spoken with a small careful woman who worked as a small local estate agent, and had, in the specific small way, told her that he was not going to sell the house.

He had, in the afternoons, at three o'clock, gone into the small back bedroom.

He had brought, each afternoon, a specific small book. He had, over the weeks, read to the small occupant of the small back bedroom a great many books. He had read the small collection of Hungarian folk tales. He had read the small collection of short stories his grandmother had, throughout his childhood, kept on the small shelf beside her small green armchair. He had read, over the small careful weeks, a small careful selection of the small novels she had loved.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man doing a small careful thing, spoken to the small occupant of the small back bedroom quietly and warmly. He had, on some afternoons, told the small occupant about his life. He had told him about London. He had told him about his small work. He had told him — quietly — about his small ex-wife, and about the small child they had, in a small terrible summer at thirty-one, lost during a small early pregnancy, and about the small quiet grief that had, in the small careful way of certain small quiet griefs, ended his small marriage.

He had told the small occupant these things because he had understood, over the small careful weeks, that the small occupant of the small back bedroom was, in the specific small careful way, a version of himself who had never grown up to know these things. Who had, in whatever small careful way, remained a small child in a small back bedroom in a small house on Nagymezo Street, and who had, in the specific small careful way of a small child, been receiving a small gradual careful education in what his adult life had, in the intervening years, contained.

The small occupant had, throughout those weeks, listened.

The small occupant had never, at any point, been visible. The small occupant had never spoken. But the small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, over the weeks, become the specific small warm quality of attention of a small child who was, in the specific small careful way, coming to trust.

Tamás had, over those weeks, become, in some specific small way, a father.

He had understood, in the specific small careful way of a man who had, over the last decade, come to accept that he was not going to be one in any ordinary way, that this was, at last, the specific small careful shape of his fatherhood.

He had been, in the specific small careful way, glad.

chapters.title: The Small Son
chapters.body:
He had kept the house.

He had, at the end of the third month, arranged with his small firm in London to work remotely from Budapest. He had, at the end of the sixth month, notified his small firm that he was going to work remotely from Budapest indefinitely. He had, at the end of the first year, quietly retired from the small firm, and had, in the specific small careful way, taken up small consulting work with a small Hungarian firm that specialized in the small careful restoration of small historic buildings.

He had lived, from then on, in the small house on Nagymezo Street.

He had, in the specific small careful way of a man doing a small careful new life, done what he had, throughout his adult life, not been able to do. He had, at forty-seven, become, in the specific small careful way, at home. He had, at forty-eight, entered into a small careful relationship with a small careful Hungarian woman he had met at a small careful function, a small woman named Ildikó who was, in the specific small careful way, a small widowed librarian at the small national library. He had, at forty-nine, married her. She had, at forty-nine, moved into the small house on Nagymezo Street.

He had, before her moving in, told her about the small back bedroom.

He had told her simply. He had told her what was there. He had told her what he had, over the previous year, done. He had asked her, in the small specific careful way, whether she was, on the whole, willing to live in a house with a small occupant in the small back bedroom whom Tamás was, in the specific small careful way, going to continue to read to.

Ildikó had, at the small kitchen table where he had told her, been quiet for a long moment.

Ildikó had said, at last: *is he happy?*

Tamás had said: *I think so.*

Ildikó had said: *does he know I am coming?*

Tamás had said: *I have told him.*

Ildikó had said: *and does he — does he mind?*

Tamás had said: *I do not think so.*

Ildikó had, at this, sat with her small careful thinking for another moment.

Ildikó had said: *may I meet him?*

Tamás had said: *he does not — he does not, in the specific small careful way, permit himself to be seen. But he will, I think, permit himself to be spoken to.*

Ildikó had said: *may I read to him too?*

Tamás had said, quietly: *I think he would like that.*

They had, that afternoon, at three, gone together into the small back bedroom. Tamás had, in the specific small careful way, introduced Ildikó to the small occupant. He had said, in the specific small quiet voice: *this is Ildikó. She is going to live with us. She is a librarian. She reads very well.*

The small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, at the introduction, done something Tamás had not, in the previous year and a half, seen it do.

It had, in the specific small careful way, moved closer.

It had, in the specific small careful way of a small child edging up to a new person to have a small closer look, come across the small room and had settled at a small position near Ildikó's small chair.

Ildikó had, at the small position, felt it.

She had, in the specific small careful way, smiled.

She had said, quietly: *hello. It is very nice to meet you.*

The small quality of attention had, at her greeting, done something further. It had, in the specific small warm careful way, *warmed.* It had, in the specific small way of a small child who had, at last, met a small kind stranger, become the specific small quality of shyness that was also, in the small specific way, welcome.

Tamás had, at the small back bedroom, understood that the small occupant had, at first meeting, liked Ildikó.

He had, in his own small careful way, been relieved.

—

They had lived, from then on, the three of them, in the small house on Nagymezo Street.

They had, over the small careful years that followed, arranged their small careful life around the small routine of the small back bedroom. Tamás had, on most afternoons, at three, gone into the small room and had read for perhaps twenty minutes. Ildikó had, on other afternoons, done the same. On some Sundays, in the small specific careful way of a small family doing a small careful weekly thing, they had, together, gone into the small room, and had sat together in the two small chairs Tamás had, over the years, arranged, and had read to the small occupant together.

The small occupant had, over the years, in the specific small careful way, grown.

Not in any small way that could have been described in ordinary language. The small occupant had continued, throughout, to be invisible. But the small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, over the years, changed. It had, over the first several years, been the specific small quality of a small child of about eight. It had, over the following several years, gradually become the specific small quality of a small child of about ten. Then twelve.

By the time Tamás had been sixty and Ildikó had been sixty-three, the small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had been the specific small quality of a small teenager of about fifteen.

Which had been, so far as Tamás had been able to tell, the specific age at which he himself, on his last summer visit, had left the small back bedroom.

—

He had, at sixty-one, on a small quiet Sunday afternoon in April, sat in the small back bedroom with the small collection of Hungarian folk tales — the same small book he had, at forty-six, first read to the small occupant — and had, in the specific small careful way, closed the small book at the end of a small story, and had said, into the small quiet:

*I think you are ready.*

The small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, at this, attended.

Tamás had said: *I think you have — you have grown, in the last fifteen years, in the small careful way of a small careful teenager. I think you are now, so far as I can tell, the small careful age of the small careful boy I was when I left this room for the last time.*

*I think it is time.*

The small quality of attention had, at this, become still.

Tamás had said, more quietly: *I have thought about this for some time. I have thought about what it means, for you to be here. I have thought about — I have thought about what would happen when you reached the small age at which I stopped coming.*

*I have understood, in the last several months, that when you reach it, you will be — you will be finished. That the specific small careful task of your being in this room was to grow, in the specific small careful way of the small child I was, to the specific small age of the small child I was on the last day I came here.*

*And after that — after that you will not, any longer, be a small child in a small back bedroom.*

*After that you will be — you will be me. You will be — you will be me at fifteen, on the last morning I came down the stairs with my small suitcase, and said goodbye to my grandmother, and left. And after that — after that you will, in the specific small careful way, go where I went. You will grow up. You will become — you will become the small careful man who has, in the last fifteen years, been coming into this room every afternoon and reading to you.*

*You will become me.*

The small quality of attention in the small back bedroom had, at this, done something Tamás had not, at any point in the fifteen years, felt.

It had, in the specific small careful way, *understood.*

It had understood in the small specific way of a small careful teenager who had, over fifteen years of small careful reading, come to understand what was, in the specific small careful way, being said to him.

Tamás had said, quietly: *and I will, in the specific small careful way, still be here. I will be here as a small older self of yours. I will be here with Ildikó.
